This model asks how words understood and words spoken develop **together** in typically-developing children over a narrow window of early infancy: not just how many words a child of a given age knows and says, but what fraction of the words they understand they also say, and how that fraction changes with age.

::: {.callout-important title="What this model is for"}

VG13 is a **reference model**. It exists to give the Down syndrome joint models — VG05 without hierarchy, VG20 with it — a typically-developing comprehension-and-production picture to be read against, and it supersedes the retired VG06.

Its relatives are worth knowing before reading any figure here. **VG04** asks the comprehension question of the same population with no study or child effects, on a subsample and an English-only pool; **VG03** is its spoken-vocabulary counterpart. **VG12** asks the comprehension question with both kinds of random effect, on the full pool, over a much wider age range. VG12 is the direct comparison for this model: where the two windows overlap, they should agree, and because they use different engines, different age ranges and different likelihoods, agreement between them is a genuine external check rather than a restatement. Disagreement with VG04 in the same region is expected and informative in the other direction — VG04 carries no hierarchy, so between-study differences reach its curve as though they were between-child differences.

**A reference is not a target.** A typically-developing trajectory describes what typically-developing children in these datasets did. It is a comparison baseline, not a goal against which an individual child with Down syndrome should be judged or an intervention scored.

:::

::: {.callout-note}

For full details and discussion, please refer to the technical report.

:::

## Statistical model

Two outcomes are modelled together. The first is the number of words a child **understands**, as a bounded count out of the reference inventory. The second is the number of words the child **speaks**, modelled not directly but as a fraction of what they understand: the production ratio $q(a) = P(\text{speak} \mid \text{understood}, a)$, so that $p_S(a) = p_U(a)\,q(a)$.

That reparameterisation is the point of the model. It enforces $p_S \le p_U$ by construction — a child cannot say more words than they understand — and it separates _knowing more words_ from _saying more of the words you know_, which two independent trajectories would confound.

Both $p_U$ and $q$ are smooth functions of age on the logit scale: a straight-line trend defined by priors at two reference ages, plus a Gaussian process term that lets each curve bend by as much as the data support and no more. Both Gaussian processes are anchored at one age between the reference ages — every posterior draw is forced to zero there — which is an identifiability device that removes the ridge along which the GP level and the intercept would otherwise trade off, not a claim that development changes at that age.

Each trajectory carries two offsets on the logit scale: one per contributing study, and one per child, both sampled in non-centred form. Non-centring is a sampler convenience and changes nothing about the model. The child offsets are what stop repeated administrations of the same child being treated as observations of different children.

Paired rows — those recording both outcomes for the same administration — use the nested factorisation $P(U)\,P(S \mid U)$: the spoken count is modelled conditionally on the **observed** understood count rather than on a modelled one. The engine also provides a marginal fallback for rows recording only spoken vocabulary, but **this fit never enters it**: the toddler form, which is the only source of spoken-only rows in this pool, is excluded for the reason given below, so every row here is fully paired and nested.

Both outcomes use a Beta-Binomial likelihood with age-varying dispersion. Because both trajectories already carry a child offset, $\kappa$ describes what is left once a child's own level is known, not the total spread between children at an age.

Population-level trajectories set both random effects to zero, so the plotted curves describe the **average study**, not any contributing study. Predictive count trajectories draw one new child's offset per posterior draw, which is why they are much the wider of the two.

Contributing datasets below a minimum observation count are dropped before fitting. This removes a sizeable fraction of the contributing studies while retaining almost all of the observations; the dropped names are printed to the fit console and are not currently written to any artefact, and this engine writes no per-study count table at all.

## Priors {#sec-priors}

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| output: asis
from vocab_growth.report_cells import render_priors_table

render_priors_table()
```

### Understood trajectory

The low-age anchor is concentrated near the floor, deliberately a little below the published norm rather than tightened onto it, because percentiles are unstable where a skill is only just emerging. The high anchor is set from the same published norms and kept clear of the comprehension form's own ceiling — an earlier, much broader setting overshot the norm by roughly a factor of two and sat against that ceiling, which is a prior asserting something the instrument cannot show.

![How far apart in age two points must be before the understood trend is allowed to move independently.](ell_unit_u_dist.png){#fig-ell-u .lightbox fig-align="left"}

![How far the flexible term may depart from the straight-line understood trend, on the logit scale.](eta_u_dist.png){#fig-eta-u .lightbox fig-align="left"}

![Prior on the proportion of the reference inventory understood at the low age anchor.](p_slope_low_u_dist.png){#fig-slope-low-u .lightbox fig-align="left"}

![Prior on the proportion of the reference inventory understood at the high age anchor.](p_slope_hi_u_dist.png){#fig-slope-hi-u .lightbox fig-align="left"}

### Production ratio

The $q(a)$ anchors are probabilities conditional on understanding, not word counts: a value of 0.25 means a child is expected to speak about one quarter of the words they understand at that age.

::: {.callout-important title="These are not the family's baseline $q$ priors"}

VG13 is the one model in the family that **rejected** the shared bivariate production-ratio baseline, and the rejection was made on measured evidence rather than taste.

That baseline is tuned to the much older and wider Down syndrome age window. Applied to a young typically-developing population it sits far above the ratio these children actually show, and because spoken vocabulary is the product of the understood trajectory and the ratio, the two errors compound: the prior predicted spoken vocabularies several times larger than anything observed. VG13 therefore uses window-appropriate anchors set at or just below the floor implied by published norms — the ratio of median production to median comprehension in the norming data — rather than the family default. The priors table above gives the settings; `docs/models/PRIORS.md` records their derivation.

The GP amplitude on $q$ is a second deliberate departure. The family widened it because the logit of $q$ is S-shaped across the full Down syndrome age range and the GP is the only term that can carry that curvature. Over this model's narrow young window only the bottom limb of that S is in view, so the amplitude prior is deliberately narrow here — `eta_q_sigma = 0.2`, against 0.5 for VG21 over the wider 8–22-month window and 0.8 in the Down syndrome models. The posterior does not press against it: it sits at the 57th percentile of that prior, so the data are content within it and widening it would buy nothing. **That agreement must not be read as the data choosing this amplitude.** Its prior-to-posterior contraction is 0.004 and the diagnostic flags it `uninformed` — the least informed $q$ amplitude in the family, against 0.54–0.59 in every Down syndrome model. VG23, over the same window with the same prior, behaves identically (57th percentile, contraction 0.008). The narrow prior and the silent data agree; neither is evidence about curvature. See [Limits](#sec-limits) and the GP-inertness paragraph below. A reader comparing this model's $q$ band against a Down syndrome model's should know the two amplitudes differ substantially, and in which direction.

:::

![How far apart in age two points must be before the production ratio is allowed to move independently.](ell_unit_q_dist.png){#fig-ell-q .lightbox fig-align="left"}

![How far the flexible term may depart from the straight-line production-ratio trend, on the logit scale. This is the narrowed prior described above.](eta_q_dist.png){#fig-eta-q .lightbox fig-align="left"}

![Prior on the production ratio at the low age anchor.](p_slope_low_q_dist.png){#fig-slope-low-q .lightbox fig-align="left"}

![Prior on the production ratio at the high age anchor.](p_slope_hi_q_dist.png){#fig-slope-hi-q .lightbox fig-align="left"}

### Random effects

The study and child random-effect scales are regularising rather than informative: they expect datasets and children to differ, but not wildly, and let the data say how much. The study offsets enter the likelihood and are set to zero in the reported population-level curves, so those curves describe the average study.

### Dispersion

Both outcomes follow `kappa(age) = kappa_min + exp(a_kappa + b_kappa * z)`, with the age term given priors at two reference ages rather than as an intercept at the pool's mean age plus a slope, so neither prior shifts meaning if the pool's age distribution changes. Because this model carries study and child offsets on both trajectories, the anchors are calibrated on the **conditional** scale — the spread left once a child's own level is known — which is a much smaller quantity than the raw spread between children at an age. The priors table above gives the settings.

The two outcomes get deliberately different treatment. The understood dispersion is expected to rise across this window, which the earlier parameterisation could not represent at any setting; its floor parameter is correspondingly a _young_-age asymptote rather than a floor, since a rising exponential term contributes almost nothing below the young anchor and a substantial part of this frame sits there. The per-age profile behind the rise is jagged, so both understood anchors take a wider prior than the production-ratio ones.

::: {.callout-note title="Why a rising $\\kappa$ on understood is not a statement about children"}

Understood counts come from forms holding far fewer items than the common reference inventory, but are scored against that inventory. As children work up a form, the modelled proportion compresses towards a value the instrument cannot exceed, so the apparent between-child spread _on the logit scale_ falls across this window. The child offset's scale is fixed in age and cannot follow that, so $\kappa$ absorbs the difference.

The production ratio shows none of this, and that is the check on the explanation rather than a coincidence: its denominator is the child's own understood count, so the form cancels. That is why its two anchors are near-equal and take the narrower prior — and why, if the two dispersion curves behave differently in the Findings section, the difference is telling you about the measurement scale rather than about development.

:::

## Prior predictive checks {#sec-prior-predictive}

These simulate vocabularies from the priors alone, before the data are seen, and should be read against this model's deliberately narrow target window. The test has four criteria: rapid early comprehension growth should be permitted but not forced; spoken counts should stay low to moderate; trajectories should be smooth; and $q(a)$ should stay within the range a young typically-developing child could plausibly occupy. The last of these is the one that failed under the family's baseline ratio priors and drove the change described in the Priors section, so these figures are the direct evidence for that decision.

![Trajectories for words understood drawn from the priors.](prior_samples_u.png){#fig-prior-samples-u .lightbox fig-align="left"}

![Trajectories for words spoken implied by those priors, as the product of the understood trajectory and the production ratio.](prior_samples_s.png){#fig-prior-samples-s .lightbox fig-align="left"}

![Trajectories for the production ratio $q(a)$ drawn from the priors.](prior_samples_q.png){#fig-prior-samples-q .lightbox fig-align="left"}

::: {.callout-note}

The normality tests in this table, where present, are reported for completeness. They are not a check on the model: the outcomes are bounded counts, which are not expected to be normally distributed, and the model does not assume that they are.

Note also that neither contributing form holds the whole reference inventory — both hold appreciably less of it. Counts are harmonised onto the common scale, so the observed maxima in this table fall well short of the inventory size, and the upper tail of every count figure in this report is bounded by an instrument rather than by children. This is the same fact the dispersion callout in the Priors section rests on, and it belongs in mind at every trajectory figure below, not only at the priors.

:::

::: {.callout-important title="The reference pool is not English-only"}

This model's typically-developing pool is scoped to English **and** two Romance languages, Italian and Spanish (European), so that the Down-syndrome-versus-typically-developing comparison spans several languages on both sides — the Down syndrome pool is already substantially non-English. The language scope is part of the model graph, so it is not a reporting choice: changing it requires a refit.

Language is very nearly collinear with dataset here: each added language enters through its own contributing dataset, so a language effect cannot be separated from a sample effect. The project's model definitions are explicit that it must therefore be **reported as between-dataset heterogeneity**, which is what the study-effect scales in the Findings section are measuring. Part of the spread between studies reported there is language, unseparably, and neither this model nor any model in the family can tell you which part.

This engine writes no per-study table, so the datasets and their languages are not listed on this page at all. Closing that gap needs a change to the fitting engine.

:::

A fit reaching this page has therefore either met those thresholds or is published under a recorded exception — and if there is an exception, the block above states it, names the parameter, and gives the reason it was accepted. ```

::: {.callout-important title="What the energy diagnostic caveat means for this report"}

Where the caveat block above reports an energy (BFMI) shortfall, it should not be read as incidental. In this model it appears on every chain rather than on one unlucky one, which makes it a property of the posterior's geometry rather than of an individual run.

A low energy fraction means the sampler moved between energy levels more slowly than it moved within them. It is a **global** warning about how thoroughly the posterior was explored, not a diagnostic that localises the damage to any particular summary: it cannot certify that central estimates are unbiased. Poor energy exploration does tend to show first in the extremes, so preferring medians and 50% inner bounds to the 89% outer bounds is a sensible reading order — but it is a precaution, not a guarantee, and **every** posterior summary in this report remains subject to this warning until the quantities it rests on have been shown stable across independent fits or an alternative parameterisation. Where a conclusion turns on any of them, treat it as provisional.

The recorded cause in this model family is structural rather than technical: most children in the pool contribute a single administration, so there is little within-child replication from which to separate a child's own persistent level from residual spread. That is a property of the available data, and the project's own record states it is not reparameterisable away.

:::

::: {.callout-note title="Diagnostic focus, and what it found"}

The parameters to watch here are the two study-effect scales, the anchored GP hyperparameters, and the production-ratio trajectory, because weak behaviour in any of them bears directly on the comprehension-production interpretation this model exists to support. This report should not merely direct you to them and stop, so:

**The hierarchy terms are the weakest part of the fit and still clear the gate.** The lowest effective sample sizes and the highest R-hat values in the diagnostics table sit on the study-effect scales rather than on the trajectory parameters — which is what the sparse-replication problem above predicts — but they sit inside the thresholds, and the caveat block above states whether any exception was needed.

**The Gaussian processes are close to inert, and that is a limit on what this model can detect rather than evidence of linearity.** Read the amplitude and length-scale rows of the contraction table above: a contraction near zero means they were barely moved. The shared length-scale prior spans roughly 6–18 months against a ten-month window, and the anchored GP is additionally stripped of the components that mimic its mean's basis, so the model has little effective capacity to bend inside the frame in the first place — a shorter-length-scale experiment left the length scale prior-driven while costing divergences (`notes/202608060900-three-prior-conflicts.md`). The defensible reading is therefore that curvature was **not identified** under this graph: straight lines on the logit scale describe these data adequately over this window, but the fit does not demonstrate that the trajectories are straight, and the GP's inertness must not be quoted as evidence for it. It follows that the anchor priors are load-bearing here in a way they are not in the wider-window models — which is exactly why the production-ratio anchor discussion above matters, and why the registered sensitivity variants are worth running.

:::

### How much do studies and children differ?

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| output: asis

render_variation_table()
```

Each row is a standard deviation on the logit scale, with the odds reading beside it. Both outcomes carry both kinds of offset, so there are four rows: how much studies differ on comprehension and on the production ratio, and how much children do.

Read them with three things in mind. **The plotted population curves are the average study**, not any contributing study, so a comparison drawn against one particular typically-developing dataset would not give the same answer as these curves. **Part of the between-study spread is language**, as set out in the Data section, and it cannot be isolated from everything else that distinguishes those laboratories. And **the between-child rows are what make the single-child predictive bands so much wider than the mean-trajectory bands** in every figure below; they are also, per the energy caveat above, the quantities the pool's sparse repeat measurement constrains least well.

::: {.callout-note title="Sensitivity variants"}

Four deliberate one-change variants of this model are registered and can be refitted with `scripts/fit_sensitivity.py`: retaining a single administration per child with the child effects removed (`single-admin`), and three observation-window variants (`window-22`, `window-25` and `window-22-vague-anchors`). **Nothing in this report is a result from any of them.** The window pair was fitted on 2026-08-20 at this model's own reporting settings, and the study owner adopted the 8–22-month specification for the matched-comprehension comparison while rejecting 8–25 as ceiling-contaminated (`notes/202608211100-window-22-adopted.md`); its promotion as a registered successor model (VG21) is tracked in [#240](https://github.com/dseinternational/vocabulary-growth/issues/240). The `single-admin` variant has not been run — given that repeated administrations are the mechanism behind both the child scales and the energy caveat, it is the variant most worth having next.

:::

## Joint trajectory {#sec-predictions}

![Expected words understood and words spoken on the same axes, across the modelled window. The vertical distance between the two curves is the comprehension-production gap, quantified below.](joint_trajectory.png){#fig-joint-trajectory .lightbox fig-align="left"}

![Where each study sits. One curve per study over the ages it actually covers, the **reference child** (zero study and child effects — the child in the average study) in bold, and the **administration-weighted child** — the same fit re-weighted to the studies present at each age — dashed. Studies are segregated by age, so at a given age the reference child can sit above or below every study sampled there; every population figure and milestone on this page is the reference child's.](study_fans.png){#fig-study-fans .lightbox fig-align="left"}


![The same two trajectories with 50% inner and 89% outer equal-tailed intervals. These are uncertainty intervals on the zero-effect population trajectory — the typical (median) child in the typical study, which on the count scale is not the same thing as the average across children — not the range individual children occupy; for that, read the predictive figures and the monthly tables.](joint_trajectory_intervals.png){#fig-joint-trajectory-intervals .lightbox fig-align="left"}

::: {.callout-warning title="Age restriction: what it costs, and what it buys"}

VG13 is restricted to a narrow young window and **should not be used as a general typically-developing trajectory beyond it**. The upper bound is this model's own choice; the lower bound is not — it is the age floor of the typically-developing pool as a whole, so nothing here says anything about what happens below it either way.

**What the restriction rested on, and what remains of it.** The original justification — that above 18 months only a single dataset contributed usable paired observations — is obsolete: since the Romance-language extension, Italian Words & Gestures supplies paired rows to 24 months, and several hundred admissible administrations from two studies sit above the cap (694 when counted on 2026-08-20; VG12 fits every one of them). What remains is a density and measurement argument: coverage above 18 months is real but thin, and the Oxford CDI's 418-item ceiling binds increasingly from 23 months. The registered `window-22` and `window-25` variants were fitted to measure the cap's cost, and the study owner adopted the 8–22-month specification (`notes/202608211100-window-22-adopted.md`); its promotion as VG21 is tracked in [#240](https://github.com/dseinternational/vocabulary-growth/issues/240). Until that lands, this 8–18-month report remains the model of record.

**What the restriction buys**, which matters just as much and is the reason the model exists at all: inside the window every row is fully paired, drawn from several laboratories, and dense at every month. That is what makes $q(a)$ identifiable — a conditional probability needs both outcomes on the same administration, and this window is where the pool supplies them without the marginal fallback ever being used.

One qualification on "several laboratories": the contributing studies are not constant across the window. Some enter only in its lower half and some only in its upper, so the claim of multi-laboratory coverage is true on average and thinner at the two edges than in the middle. The engine writes no per-study table for this model, so that composition cannot be shown here directly.

:::

## Production ratio

The first figure shows the latent $q(a) = P(\text{speak} \mid \text{understood})$ curve: the fraction of understood words a child is expected also to say. The posterior predictive spoken-over-understood **count** ratio shown afterwards is a different quantity — it includes outcome uncertainty and the discreteness of small counts — and should not be read as the latent parameter.

## Comprehension-production gap

![The expected difference, in words, between what a child understands and what they say. A gap that is still widening at the top of the window has not begun to close within it.](comprehension_production_gap.png){#fig-comprehension-production-gap .lightbox fig-align="left"}

The headline table above gives where this gap is largest within the modelled window and how wide the interval on it is at that age. Read the location with care: if the maximum sits at the edge of the window, the model is telling you the gap was still growing when the data ran out, not that it peaks there.

## Words understood vs words spoken

![Expected spoken vocabulary against expected understood vocabulary. The curve stays below the diagonal by construction, since a child cannot say more words than they understand.](understood_vs_spoken.png){#fig-understood-vs-spoken .lightbox fig-align="left"}

![The same relationship in predictive terms, so the scatter reflects where a single child might fall rather than where the zero-effect curve sits.](understood_vs_spoken_predictive.png){#fig-understood-vs-spoken-predictive .lightbox fig-align="left"}

## Receptive to expressive (cross-sectional) {#sec-spoken-given-understood}

**How are receptive and expressive vocabulary related cross-sectionally?** The joint model links the two structurally through the production ratio $q(a) = P(\text{speak} \mid \text{understood})$: the expected number of words a child _says_ is the number they _understand_ scaled by $q(a)$,

$$\mathbb{E}[\,\text{spoken} \mid \text{understood} = N,\ \text{age} = a\,] \approx N \cdot q(a).$$

Thus $q(a)$ is an age-dependent cross-sectional conversion proportion — the expected number of words spoken per word understood under the model — not evidence that increasing a particular child's receptive vocabulary causes a corresponding expressive gain. The figure below reads the fitted association directly across the modelled window, with the shaded band the 89% interval on $q(a)$ and the dashed line marking equality of spoken and understood counts, which the reparameterisation prevents the model from crossing. The per-age posterior of $q(a)$ is tabulated under [Production ratio](#production-ratio) above.

::: {.callout-warning title="Do not read this figure off its far right"}

Each line runs across the full width of the reference inventory, but at the younger ages the model does not expect any child to be anywhere near that far along it — the monthly tables below show where the individual-child predictive range actually ends at each age. Reading a spoken-vocabulary expectation for a young child at a comprehension vocabulary that young children in this pool do not reach is extrapolating along a line the data never constrained.

:::

## Posterior predictions -- words understood

### Summary at selected ages

$p$ is the latent success probability — the underlying proportion of the reference inventory a child is expected to understand at a given age. $Ey$ is the expected count implied by $p$, and reflects uncertainty in the mean trajectory alone. $Y$ is a draw from the posterior predictive distribution, and reflects both that uncertainty **and** between-child variability, so it is much the wider of the two and it is the one to quote when asking where a single child might fall. Where the table distinguishes `p_population_*` from `p_subject_marginal_*`, the first sets the child and study effects to zero — the typical (median) child in the average study, which on the count scale is not the same thing as the average across children — and the second is where one more child might land. Intervals are equal-tailed, an 89% outer and a 50% inner.

Lower $\kappa$ means **greater** variability relative to the mean; higher $\kappa$ means less. The direction is easy to misread, so the findings table above restates it as a variance inflation factor, where a larger number means a wider spread. ## Robustness {#sec-robustness}

A conclusion that depends on one arbitrary modelling choice is not a conclusion. Registered sensitivity variants refit this model with a single deliberate change and compare the reported quantities against this fit's own 89% intervals; the comparison harness records a verdict per variant and declines to give one where the comparison is not sound. The table is read from the harness's own output, and says so when none has been computed into this output root.

```{python}
from pathlib import Path

import pandas as pd
from IPython.display import Markdown, display


def comparison_path(name):
    """Locate a comparison artefact from wherever this report is rendered."""
    for base in (Path("../../comparisons"), Path("comparisons"), Path("../comparisons")):
        candidate = base / name
        if candidate.is_file():
            return candidate
    return None


robustness_path = comparison_path("sensitivity/robustness_matrix_vg13.csv")
if robustness_path is None:
    display(Markdown(
        "_The sensitivity comparison has not been computed into this output root, "
        "so no robustness matrix is available for this render._"
    ))
else:
    robustness = pd.read_csv(robustness_path)
    wanted = ["variant", "status", "n_within_ci", "n_checked", "max_abs_delta",
              "quantities_outside_ci", "verdict", "variant_fit_utc"]
    display(robustness[[c for c in wanted if c in robustness.columns]])
```

Read the `verdict` column rather than the deltas. A variant marked robust moved nothing outside this fit's own intervals, so the reported conclusions do not depend on that choice. A variant marked **sensitive** did, and is a live caveat on the quantities it names wherever the two fits disagree. Rows whose `status` records no fit have not been run.

## Out-of-sample prediction {#sec-loo}

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| output: asis
from vocab_growth.report_cells import render_loo_section

render_loo_section()
```


Read any over-coverage here alongside the between-child scales in the Findings section rather than as a separate finding. The predictive distribution integrates over a **new** child's offset, so it is necessarily wider than the scatter of the observed rows, which come from children the model has already seen. The larger the between-child scale, the larger that difference — so a hierarchical model of this kind is expected to over-cover in-sample, and the calibration section's own caveat says so.

## Limits {#sec-limits}

- **A reference, not a target.** These curves describe typically-developing children in these datasets. They are the baseline the Down syndrome models are compared against, and must not be read as a standard an individual child is failing to meet.
- **A narrow window, deliberately.** This model says nothing about ages outside the range in the glance callout above, in either direction, and should not be extended to them. For the comprehension trajectory over a much wider range, use VG12; VG04 is the no-hierarchy, English-only, subsampled predecessor of both.
- **The population curves are the average study.** They are not the curves of any contributing dataset, and the study composition is not constant across the window.
- **Language and dataset cannot be separated.** The pool spans English, Italian and Spanish (European), and each non-English language enters through a single dataset, so any language effect is reported as between-dataset heterogeneity and cannot be isolated.
- **Interval bounds are the weakest numbers on this page**, wherever the diagnostics section reports an energy shortfall — as it does for this fit, on every chain. Medians are then the most reliable summaries and the outer interval endpoints the least.
- **The Gaussian processes are close to inert.** The anchor priors are therefore doing more of the work than in the wider-window models, and the registered sensitivity variant that would test this has not been run.
- **$q(a)$ is a conversion proportion, not a mechanism.** It does not say that raising a child's comprehension would raise their production by the corresponding amount.
- **The reference inventory is a harmonisation.** Counts from different checklists are placed on a common scale; it is a unit of measurement, not an instrument any child sat, and both contributing forms reach well under its top.
- **Repeated measurement is sparse.** Most children contribute a single administration, which limits how well persistent between-child differences can be separated from residual dispersion.
